name: Ollama
notable_features: `ollama pull <model>` and it handles download, quantization choice, Modelfile templating and serving — the lowest-friction path from a model name to an API.

Bundles its own llama.cpp fork, tracked in the repo as a submodule with an explicit LLAMA_CPP_VERSION pin file. It also carries MLX and MLX-C as vendored components and has MLX-specific packages, which is why the Apple path is not purely llama.cpp.
A scheduler that keeps multiple models resident and uses VRAM data reported by the GPU libraries to decide what to keep loaded and what to evict.
Exposes OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoints alongside its native API.
Works on CPU-only and CPU-only-with-no-GPU-at-all machines; the GPU is optional.
hardware_caveats: Ollama bundles its own llama.cpp fork rather than tracking upstream continuously — the LLAMA_CPP_VERSION pin is the authoritative record of which upstream commit it is on. Expect a lag between an upstream llama.cpp release and the Ollama release carrying it.
NVIDIA: compute capability 5.0+ and driver 550+; compute capability 5.0-6.2 requires driver 570+. Anything older needs a source build.

AMD: requires the ROCm v7 driver on Linux and a ROCm v7 / HIP7-capable stack on Windows, and the ROCm library does not cover every AMD GPU. The docs give an explicit escape hatch — HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=10.3.0 to run an unsupported card on a nearby LLVM target — and list the supported targets (gfx908, gfx90a, gfx942, gfx950, gfx1030, gfx1100/1101/1102, gfx1150/1151, gfx1200/1201).
Vulkan is the widest-coverage GPU path and is enabled by default when installed: it covers Intel and AMD cards ROCm does not, and works on Windows and Linux. Disable with OLLAMA_VULKAN=0.

The scheduler depends on VRAM data the GPU libraries report. Under Vulkan, exposing that needs extra capabilities or root; without it Ollama falls back to approximate model sizes for best-effort scheduling. On Linux, AMD users may also need to add the ollama user to the render group, and SELinux can block container access to GPU devices.
Mixed iGPU/dGPU systems: the docs recommend keeping Vulkan enabled but pointing GGML_VK_VISIBLE_DEVICES at the discrete GPU index, because the iGPU's Vulkan path can be unstable.
Linux suspend/resume can make NVIDIA GPU discovery fail and silently fall back to CPU; the documented workaround is reloading nvidia_uvm.
best_for: Getting from 'I want to run this model' to a working API in one command — nothing else in this list is this easy.
Single-user laptop and desktop chat across mixed hardware, including machines with no supported CUDA or ROCm path.
Switching between several small models quickly — the resident-model scheduler makes this cheap.
AMD users on a card ROCm does not list: Vulkan just works.
App integration where an OpenAI-compatible endpoint at a fixed port is the integration contract.
avoid_for: Chasing peak tok/s — it is a distribution layer, and the bundled llama.cpp fork is a pin, not a tuning surface.
Production multi-tenant serving with paged KV and per-request scheduling policy.
Cases where you must be on the very latest llama.cpp kernels or quantization types.
Air-gapped environments with no registry access; the model pull path is the product.
notes: The scheduling field is deliberately non-standard to be honest: Ollama's scheduler is about which models stay resident in VRAM across requests (load/evict), not about batching sequences within one model the way vLLM/SGLang/TGI do. 'none-within-a-sequence' is my wording, not the project's; a reader looking for continuous batching will not find it here. No quantitative throughput claim is recorded because the docs make none. The llama.cpp-vs-fork lag is inferred from the LLAMA_CPP_VERSION pin mechanism plus the project's own bundling practice, not from an explicit statement in the docs — treat the direction as certain and the magnitude as unmeasured.
